title: The Legal Industry's Shared AI Evaluation Framework
author: Anna Guo · Elgar Weijtmans · Roel Schrijvers · Sunny Kim

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: The source accepts the need for structured, evidence-based legal-AI evaluation and materially extends it into a practitioner-led procurement framework covering strategic fit, workflow integration and real-world usability. It proposes an open-access playbook rather than demonstrating that the framework improves procurement outcomes or establishes production competence.
qs: ## The Solution: The Legal AI Evaluation Framework  The Legal AI Evaluation Framework is the legal community's first open-access evaluation framework built to help legal teams make defensible, evidence-based procurement decisions.
Functionality** — User interface design, workflow integration, customisation, input handling, and real-world usability within existing technology stacks and processes.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition by translating task-specific, reliable delivery into a staged procurement process: initial screening, validation of vendor claims, and evidence-based pilots using real workflows. It also broadens evaluation beyond output quality to security, privacy, vendor risk, adoption support and total ownership costs. These are recommendations rather than demonstrated outcome improvements.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source operationalises the cluster’s call for selective, use-context-specific deployment through a staged procurement toolkit that assesses output robustness and operational risks, culminating in evidence-based pilots using real workflows. Its security, privacy, adoption, cost and multidisciplinary criteria also concretely extend the cluster’s governance and operating-model recommendations, although lifecycle maintenance remains unresolved.

kp.k: Legal AI procurement lacks structured, evidence-based assessment
kp.d: The authors argue that legal teams lack an established playbook for hiring AI agents, struggle to differentiate vendors promising similar capabilities, and sometimes evaluate tools without IT or security involvement. They attribute duplicated effort and inconsistent decisions to this gap. The supplied text omits the numerical values behind its procurement-problem statements, so it provides no quantified prevalence for these problems.
qs: Legal teams have well-established playbooks for hiring humans, but none for hiring AI agents.
Many procurement decisions happen without a structured technical review.
The result: months of duplicated effort, inconsistent evaluation, and decisions driven by demos and marketing rather than evidence.

kp.k: Shared procurement criteria draw on international practitioner input
kp.d: The document presents the framework as an independent, open-access approach to defensible procurement, reporting input from 100+ legal leaders across 82 organizations and law firms in 25 countries and 100 evaluation sub-tests across eight criteria. These are reported participation and framework-design figures, rather than measured evidence that the framework improves procurement outcomes.
qs: The Legal AI Evaluation Framework is the legal community's first open-access evaluation framework built to help legal teams make defensible, evidence-based procurement decisions.
100+ — Legal leaders across 82 organizations and law firms
25 — Countries represented
100 — Evaluation sub-tests across 8 core criteria
**Independent** — No vendor sponsorship or commercial influence.

kp.k: Strategic fit and usability require context-specific evaluation
kp.d: The framework recommends assessing AI against the purchasing legal team's use cases, jurisdictions, languages, existing systems and long-term needs. Functionality includes workflow integration, customisation and practical usability, rather than simply whether a tool advertises a particular capability.
qs: **1. Strategic Fit** — Alignment to legal use cases, IT systems, jurisdictions, languages, and long-term legal team needs.
**2. Functionality** — User interface design, workflow integration, customisation, input handling, and real-world usability within existing technology stacks and processes.

kp.k: Output robustness extends beyond factual accuracy
kp.d: The authors recommend evaluating completeness, instruction fidelity, verifiability, citation quality and consistency across legal tasks alongside factual accuracy. This is a proposed assessment standard, not a report of measured performance or hallucination rates for any tool.
qs: **3. Robustness** — Factual accuracy, completeness, instruction fidelity, verifiability, citation quality, and consistency of AI-generated outputs across legal tasks.

kp.k: Security and privacy require distinct AI-specific scrutiny
kp.d: The framework separates security assessment from data privacy assessment. It calls for scrutiny of architecture, data flows, retrieval boundaries, adversarial resistance and organizational security alignment, while privacy review covers no-training restrictions on aggregated and derived data, deletion, localisation, vector embeddings and sub-processors.
qs: **4. Security** — Architecture and data flow transparency, access control, retrieval boundaries, adversarial resistance, AI safety, and alignment with the organisation's security policy requirements.
**5. Data Privacy** — Data use restrictions (including no-training provisions covering aggregated and derived data), deletion, localisation, vector embedding governance, and sub-processor practices.

kp.k: Vendor evaluation includes contractual and operational continuity risks
kp.d: The authors recommend assessing the provider relationship as well as the software: licensing, contractual security obligations, portability, auditability, transparency, track record, business continuity and incident response all form part of vendor risk.
qs: **6. Vendor Risk** — Licensing, contractual security commitments, data portability, audit trails, transparency, vendor track record, business continuity, and incident response.

kp.k: Adoption requires support and internal operational capacity
kp.d: The framework treats training, documentation, support, issue resolution and usage reporting as procurement considerations supporting sustained adoption. It also recommends examining pricing, total ownership costs and the buyer's capacity to deploy and maintain the tool, rather than price alone.
qs: **7. Adoption Support** — Training, support, issue resolution, documentation, and usage reporting to support rollout and sustained adoption.
**8. Cost & Resourcing** — Pricing model, total cost of ownership, and internal operational capacity required to deploy and maintain the tool.

kp.k: Staged evaluation culminates in real-workflow pilot evidence
kp.d: Using human hiring as an analogy, the authors propose progressively deeper scrutiny: pass/fail screening before a demo, scored validation during the demo, and weighted evaluation through a pilot using real workflows. Each stage produces a proceed-or-stop decision; this is a recommended procurement process rather than evidence of autonomous replacement of lawyers.
qs: Like hiring a knowledge worker, each stage of evaluating a legal AI tool demands a different level of scrutiny.
**Stage 1 · Resume screening — Pre-Demo Checklist.** Pass/fail screening to decide if a demo is worth booking. Proceed / Do Not Proceed.
**Stage 2 · Interview — Demo Scorecard.** Scored validation of whether the tool performs as claimed. Proceed / Do Not Proceed.
**Stage 3 · Working trial — Pilot Scorecard.** Evidence-based, weighted evaluation using real workflows. Proceed / Do Not Proceed.

kp.k: Evaluation should adapt to buyers and changing technology
kp.d: The framework applies to new purchases, ongoing vendor discussions, pilots and contract reassessment or renewal. The authors recommend adapting criteria to team priorities rather than treating the toolkit as rigid. They report development in November to December 2025, community feedback completed February 21, 2026, and public release on March 11, 2026, with continuing revision as tools, models and markets change.
qs: Reassessing or renewing a contract with your current provider
Adapt criteria based on your team's priorities. The toolkits are starting points, not rigid templates.
**Framework Development — Complete — November to December 2025.**
**Community Feedback — Complete — February 21, 2026.**
**Publication and Launch — Live — March 11, 2026.**
This is a living framework. It will evolve as the tools, the models, and the market change.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors claim that legal AI procurement lacks established assessment practices, producing duplicated work and marketing-led decisions; they present a shared evaluation framework as a way to make procurement evidence-based.
pts.d: Anna Guo, Elgar Weijtmans, Roel Schrijvers and Sunny Kim frame the change primarily as a procurement and governance challenge, rather than predicting lawyer displacement or changes in legal fees. They state that many legal teams are still seeking suitable tools, that many procurement decisions lack structured technical review, and that similar vendor promises make comparison difficult. Their proposed response is an adaptable framework with 100 sub-tests across eight criteria and progressively deeper screening, demonstration and real-workflow pilot stages. Its claimed benefit is defensible procurement decisions, not a demonstrated improvement in AI performance. The source also calls it the legal community's first open-access evaluation framework.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis offered is practitioner experience and community input, rather than reported comparative outcome data.
pts.d: The authors report participation by more than 100 legal leaders across 82 organizations and law firms in 25 countries. They say the framework synthesised approaches used in actual vendor selection and incorporated community feedback. Guo's biography reports benchmarking alongside more than 500 legal professionals over the preceding 13 months and influencing hundreds of procurement decisions; Weijtmans's biography reports evaluating more than 40 tools the previous year. These are experience-based credentials, not disclosed benchmark results or evidence that using the framework improves procurement outcomes. The static capture contains incomplete quantitative statements about vendor commitment, IT/security involvement and the number of tools, so no percentages or market totals can be extracted. The source asserts independence from vendor sponsorship but supplies no further funding detail in the captured text.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The diagnosis concerns the contemporary legal AI market; the framework launched in March 2026 and is intended to evolve and be adapted to individual teams.
pts.d: The source dates initial development to November–December 2025, community feedback to February 21, 2026, v1 finalisation to late February 2026, and publication to March 11, 2026. Further resources and feedback gathering are ongoing from March 2026. Applicability spans new searches, existing vendor discussions, pilots and renewals. Teams starting from scratch are advised to use all three stages in order, but the authors explicitly qualify the toolkit as a starting point rather than a rigid template. No quantified forecast, delivery deadline for procurement benefits, or long-term labour-market prediction is offered.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are legal AI buyers and their legal, IT, security and privacy colleagues; vendors face broader scrutiny of performance, risk, support and cost.
pts.d: The framework principally addresses legal teams purchasing or renewing AI tools, with participation also reported from law firms. It asks buyers to assess suitability across jurisdictions and languages, workflow integration, output quality, security, privacy, contractual and continuity risks, adoption support, and deployment resources. This expands the proposed procurement assessment beyond demonstrations of legal functionality. Vendors are the subjects of screening, demonstration validation and pilot comparison; the document does not establish the resulting compliance burden or market impact. References to output verifiability and citation quality are assessment criteria, not measured hallucination rates or evidence of reduced human verification work. No concrete effect on access to justice, client outcomes, staffing or professional employment is claimed.
